abstract: As of September 2026, artificial intelligence is creating more jobs than it destroys in the American economy. Despite initial concerns about technological unemployment, the U.S. added 162,000 jobs in August 2026 with unemployment at 4.1%, and The Economist estimates AI has created approximately 1 million new jobs since mid-2023, far exceeding the roughly 200,000 AI-related layoffs during the same period. Job creation is concentrated in data-center infrastructure, technical roles, and AI-specific positions, with emerging productivity gains potentially supporting additional employment in professional services.
keyFindings: The U.S. economy added 162,000 jobs in August 2026, with unemployment at 4.1%, lower than in nearly 90% of months over the past 50 years, with young workers (20-24-year-olds) showing unemployment rates near multi-decade lows.
AI has created approximately 1 million new jobs in America, compared to roughly 200,000 AI-related layoffs announced since mid-2023, according to The Economist's estimate.

Data-center construction spending increased by roughly $500 billion annually above 2022 levels, with data-center construction alone proceeding at over $75 billion annually, up nearly 60% year-over-year, creating demand for electricians, HVAC specialists, grid engineers, and technicians.

Employment in five data-center-related industries rose by approximately 320,000 more than broader construction and manufacturing trends would suggest since 2023, with nearly 500,000 data-center jobs created between 2023-2025.

White-collar AI-specific roles have doubled since 2023-24, with roughly 1% of professional jobs now classified as AI jobs and 4-5% of computer and life sciences occupations; meanwhile, routine-task jobs like customer-service workers and secretaries have declined 10-15% since January 2023.
methodology: The Economist conducted original tracking of five industries central to data-center build-out from 2023 onward and compared employment growth against broader construction and manufacturing trends. Analysis draws on Bureau of Labor Statistics employment data (September 2026 jobs report, wage data through June 2026, and occupational projections to 2035), Indeed job posting data, LinkedIn career history databases and hiring reports, Goldman Sachs analysis of annual infrastructure spending, Census Bureau data-center construction figures, and preliminary research by Gad Levanon of the Burning Glass Institute using career history databases to identify AI-specific jobs. Time period covered: primarily 2023-2025 with some longer-term context from 2015-2019 and projections through 2035.
qualifiers: The Economist notes that 'not all of those jobs owe their existence to AI' given that grid upgrades and other factory building also contribute to employment. Levanon's research is described as 'preliminary' and relies 'mostly on LinkedIn career histories.' The analysis explicitly states that AI 'will not have created every single one' of the 730,000 jobs added among engineers, software developers, mathematicians and data scientists above trend. Wage data comparing data-center work to comparable work elsewhere comes from Indeed, which notes data-center vacancies may not perfectly represent broader market conditions as job postings overall have fallen.
